title: Where Punk Came From, and Why It Faded Away | QDaily Anthropology
excerpt: In music and in fashion alike, punk was a way to express anger. So where have all the angry people gone?
body:
In music and in fashion alike, punk was a way to express anger. So where have all the angry people gone?

In 2008, on the day before the National Day holiday, Avril Lavigne moved her solo concert from Chengdu to the Olympic Sports Center in Chongqing's Jiulongpo District, because aftershocks were still shaking Wenchuan in Sichuan.

At the time, the Canadian singer known as the "Princess of Punk" had not long been married to the frontman of another famous pop-punk band, [Sum 41](http://baike.baidu.com/view/71088.htm). On an early-autumn night in the mountain city, the newlywed Avril bounced around the stage, still singing: "Hey! Hey! You! You! I want to be your girlfriend!"

That song, *The Best Damn Thing*, a pop-punk ode to romance, was a huge hit. To make it bigger still, Avril recorded the chorus in Chinese, French and several other languages and shot videos for them.

But understand this: if punk was ever trying to say something, it was not in Avril's lyrics, nor in Sum 41's videos of the band striking poses on a rooftop. Punk is anger, the most direct and simplest outlet for the rebellion young people feel inside.

You can stop being young in years, but as long as you keep the youth and the anger inside you, you are still a punk. Sadly, such people are becoming rarer.

## Punk as music: simple to play, hard to classify

Musically, punk is simple and loose. A simple but catchy melody, three chords, fast drums and hard strumming: that is punk. "We just wanted kids to watch the Ramones and feel they could do it too," said Johnny Ramone, the band's guitarist. "Not like the '60s, when you'd watch Jeff Beck or Jimi Hendrix and think you'd have to practice for 20 years to play like that."

![The Ramones](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607021608146CDXl2kRHuZP4wI0.jpg-w600)

Beyond the beat itself, though, punk seems to resist definition. It has one core meaning: angry revolt. The Scottish singer Shirley Manson once joked: "If rebellion is what makes punk, then Mozart was probably a punk too. He was so mischievous, so out of step with his time."

Avril meets neither test. The flashy effects on her records, the pop vocals and arrangements, the loud marketing, even the hi-fi polish: none of it is punk. People usually call her pop-punk.

In the early days, punks refused to count pop-punk as punk at all. By punk's own definition as something outside the mainstream, it had no business mixing with "pop," and they insisted that commercialization would destroy the movement's ideals.

After the original punk of the 1970s, 1980s America produced hardcore, known for being extremely fast, simple and raw; it slowly faded because it was too violent and too underground. Skate punk, street punk and emo followed.

Pop-punk rose in the '90s. Its start is usually dated to Nirvana's breakthrough into the mainstream, but the style really took off after Green Day released *Dookie* in 1994. The wave was centered on California's Bay Area, and its leading bands included Green Day, the Offspring, Bad Religion, Rancid and Pennywise.

China had punk too, more than a decade ago: Beijing's "Bored Army" (Wuliao Contingent). Dozens of bands in that scene, among them Brain Failure, Reflector, 69 and Anarchy Boys, played China's earliest punk. Today they have either broken up or, like Reflector, moved on to pop-punk.

![Green Day: *Dookie*](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702160815lTj7ut54dev3fRHC.jpg-w600)

Pop-punk borrowed punk's rhythm, but its spirit is entirely different: affected and vain.

## Real punk is a form of cultural expression

Punk emerged in the 1970s among the working class of America and Britain, a youth movement in the full sense. Its members chose the English word "punk" to set themselves apart from mainstream society: young and stubborn, bored, cheap, worthless. They began with music to express their attitude toward life and their refusal to be tamed; later the movement spread to clothing, design, comics and beyond.

That era truly belonged to the young. Birth rates were high worldwide and populations were exploding. Europe showed it most clearly. By the mid-1960s, young people seemed to be everywhere: in France in 1968, students aged 16 to 24 numbered more than 8 million, 16.1% of the population. By 1960, 30% of the people in the Netherlands, Ireland and Finland were under 15.

The young of that era had problems of their own. In earlier times, such a population boom would have strained the food supply, and even if everyone could be fed, finding them work would have been hard. But in a period of fast growth and prosperity, teenagers' main problem was not food, clothing or housing, nor even jobs. It was how to get an education.

This was the backdrop to punk: the world suddenly had a great many more young people. Before the world could teach them to see things as adults did, they were old enough to make sense of it themselves. To them, middle-class life was not the satisfying thing their parents saw; it was the boredom that follows comfort. Society did not take them seriously, and they were eager to show they were different from those before them. They wanted to state their own views and defy their parents. Their thinking was about the here and now. They wanted to rebel.

In modern intellectual history, the years from the 1960s to the 1980s are also called the era of "revolt and reaction." It was in this period that student movements broke out across East and West, with mass unrest and uprisings: the "Red May" of Paris in 1968, the student movement in Japan, and others. Students demanded changes to the social order, boycotted classes and marched in the streets. Events in China at that time also transformed the country completely, though of course not only because of the young.

![June 15, 1960: Japan's "Day of Bloody Protest"](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607021608168tr7en2yLFI15SYc.jpg-w600)

The 1970s also came right after the hippie movement. People had just been through "love and peace," and rock had just taken over from the blues as the main music of teenagers. The people who made proto-punk, such as the Who, the Velvet Underground and Iggy Pop, were themselves figures of the hippie era. The doors of perception had opened for teenagers and self-awareness had taken root. They had learned to understand the world in their own way and to express it in their own way.

But after watching the hippie movement fail, young people stopped dreaming of a life of "love and peace" and stopped building themselves on idealism alone. Instead they pushed self-expression further than ever: no talk of ideals, just criticism and defiance through the sharpest sarcasm, the crudest words and the strangest clothes. Life was not a bed of flowers; it was "No Fun," as Iggy Pop sang. Nor was there the bright future adults had promised. At the end of their most famous song, "God Save the Queen," the Sex Pistols screamed: "No future, no future for you, no future for me."

![Cover of "God Save the Queen"](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702160816ZMxqRAstdeGgS5aQ.jpg-w600)

That is the setting in which punk became young people's declaration of war on middle-class life.

## Who becomes a punk

In 2007, the American punk fan Susan Dynner released her documentary *Punk's Not Dead*. In it, David Vanian, the singer of the Damned, says he worked as a gravedigger for a year before he took up punk. Joe Strummer, singer and guitarist of the Clash, says: "If there were good jobs, we wouldn't be playing punk. Maybe we'd even be singing sweet nothings."

Strummer also said: "Punk is rebel rock, and it belongs to the young. It's not a bunch of old guys playing music for your mum and dad. It's working-class music. It has nothing to do with the middle class or the road warriors."

That was the first punk: a way for working-class youth to vent their anger. Everyone had a band. No experience? You could still start one. No instrument? If you could shout, that was enough. You didn't need musical talent, only the will. All kinds of socialism and anarchism got mixed in. Teenagers got together and brought their own songs; the form didn't matter, and the message was always the same: we listen only to ourselves. Joey Ramone, the Ramones' singer, described their music like this: "It's about our loneliness and isolation. Just feelings."

The feeling may have been more complicated than loneliness, because once it was sung, it came out as "Hey, ho, let's go!" That urgent, furious line comes from the Ramones' "Blitzkrieg Bop," one of their best-known songs.

Across the Atlantic in Britain was a band that may have been angrier still: the Sex Pistols. In the summer of 1978, the Sex Pistols released "God Save the Queen" and, on the day of Queen Elizabeth II's Silver Jubilee, marking 25 years on the throne, played it at a concert on a boat on the Thames. It was the most biting satire of the British dream: they did the most fearless thing with the most careless attitude. Singer Johnny Rotten called it "a rose for the fools."

![Queen Elizabeth II's Silver Jubilee](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702160817RqUSvVG1oFJ6Zjp7.jpg-w600)

But not all punk was this blunt. Patti Smith was an outlier in the scene. Her music was closer to poetry, and her performances were poetry performed. When she closed her eyes, the words poured out. She seemed to have stepped out of the '60s hippie world, except that she turned its poetry into three-chord punk. Some called her music "art punk." In plain, direct words, she sang: "Jesus died for somebody's sins, but not mine."

## In music and in fashion, commerce killed punk

By late 1976, the British media had set out to crush punk. The Sex Pistols appeared on a TV news talk show where the host kept mocking them, treating them as a gang of hooligans rather than serious musicians. The band and their friends first insisted, sincerely, that they took their music seriously, then hit the host with a barrage of swearing on air.

![The Sex Pistols and friends on Thames Television's "Today"](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702160818y5IFDwbUgC10KPSk.jpg-w600)

The early movement was rebellious and scornful, like a rebirth of the rock spirit, and big business had not yet noticed it. In fact, the major labels knew nothing about it, and none would sign a punk band. They saw punk as trash and as a risk, not as an opportunity.

Punk bands didn't even bother approaching those labels; doing it yourself was the norm. In Manchester, the Buzzcocks made the first DIY punk record, *Spiral Scratch*. Recording took half an hour and cost 500 pounds. The lo-fi sound that came from such a cheap recording even became a hallmark of punk. Pete Shelley of the band said of the record: "We didn't set out to make it that way, but it fits the punk creed. You can do it yourself, nothing can stop you, even if it's not shiny and perfect... I think its value is in the imperfection. That's a truer picture of life."

But in the end, punk was commercialized.

In the late 1980s, grunge, the punk music of America's Pacific Northwest, appeared. Its leading bands, Nirvana and Pearl Jam, were commercial successes, and that success carried another punk style into the mainstream, known as power pop or pop-punk. In 1991, punk exploded. Nirvana sold 5 to 6 million records; then came the Offspring, then Green Day, who were even nominated for a Grammy. Punk had become a commercial phenomenon in America.

By 1996, commerce and punk were closer still, but the bands were torn between the money commerce brought to the music and the contempt of the punk crowd.

One key figure here is Kevin Lyman, who founded 4Fini, a company that organizes live music festivals. Its best-known product is the [Warped Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vans_Warped_Tour), a large annual open-air [music festival](https://www.baidu.com/s?wd=%E9%9F%B3%E4%B9%90%E8%8A%82&tn=44039180_cpr&fenlei=mv6quAkxTZn0IZRqIHckPjm4nH00T1Y1mWIBPyFBrHfLmvfkP1I-0ZwV5Hcvrjm3rH6sPfKWUMw85HfYnjn4nH6sgvPsT6KdThsqpZwYTjCEQLGCpyw9Uz4Bmy-bIi4WUvYETgN-TLwGUv3ErjR3n1bsn1R) that sometimes added extreme-sports competitions, making it an all-round outdoor [music festival](https://www.baidu.com/s?wd=%E9%9F%B3%E4%B9%90%E8%8A%82&tn=44039180_cpr&fenlei=mv6quAkxTZn0IZRqIHckPjm4nH00T1Y1mWIBPyFBrHfLmvfkP1I-0ZwV5Hcvrjm3rH6sPfKWUMw85HfYnjn4nH6sgvPsT6KdThsqpZwYTjCEQLGCpyw9Uz4Bmy-bIi4WUvYETgN-TLwGUv3ErjR3n1bsn1R).

In 1996 the tour drew a large number of punk bands. Vans and the retailer Target rushed in as sponsors. The punks were wary at first, but decided it might be a way to make a better living.

"This is the best tour we've done," said Jake Kolatis of the Casualties. "Honestly, I can't say what's bad about them. They're not everything. Get on board, make more money, that's how it should be. Using what the industry gives you for free beats starting from nothing. That doesn't work anymore. This way there's still a chance to make money."

That was more or less how a later generation of punks thought: they hoped business would give them a leg up. In 2006, the department store Selfridges went as far as staging a punk-themed celebration, declaring: "Selfridges is the punk of the future."

Meanwhile, punk style became fashion, and plenty of brands wanted to mine the subculture for profit. As in music, true punks sneered at the fashion world and its imitations.

Fashion magazines even ran punk guides along the lines of "Dress Like a Punk in Six Steps," so that pop culture could spread the punk spirit more easily.

The original punk look meant piercing the face; ripping clothes and holding them together with safety pins or straps; painting and decorating clothes; wearing black bin bags as shirts or dresses; and using safety pins and razor blades as jewelry. Punks also deliberately wore leather, rubber and vinyl, materials that suggested crime, sexual violence and fetish. In short, the look was extreme, unruly and provocative.

The clothes also reflected the music. Punks singing in a rage would tear their jeans, and sneakers, leather jackets and T-shirts printed with provocative slogans also became signatures of punk fashion.

But the people buying these cool-looking clothes may not grasp this; they think the clothes are the whole story. Take Patti Smith again, the scene's outlier. The cover of her famous album *Horses* is a photo of her in a man's shirt and braces, a man's jacket slung over her shoulder, tie loose, her expression firm: a woman full of confidence. No clutter of accessories, no piercings, no studs. Punks simply dressed to look more like themselves, whatever others thought.

![Cover of Patti Smith's *Horses*](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702160818UZSGxCeibPfFhY56.jpg-w600)

In the history of punk fashion, Vivienne Westwood, known to Chinese fans as the "Empress Dowager," is a central figure. Her anger often turned political (but whose doesn't? Sometimes it works). Last September at London Fashion Week, she turned the show for her Red Label diffusion line into a street protest denouncing the ugly faces of politicians.

There is no need to retell her punk history at length. She was once the girlfriend of Malcolm McLaren, and the way the two of them lived and dressed fit the anarchism that swept 1970s Britain.

Take the clothing shop they opened in 1974 called SEX (later renamed Seditionaries). Its door bore the pensive line: "Clothes make the man, but truth loves to go naked." It sold punk fashion, much of it designed by Westwood herself, and the Sex Pistols were regulars.

Rubber clothing and bondage trousers sold briskly, and they made Vivienne Westwood's name. The pair also launched a fashion for T-shirts bearing provocative slogans, such as "Cambridge Rapist" and "Paedophile." The most famous was a T-shirt printed with "God Save the Queen," with a safety pin through the Queen's nose.

American and British punk never agreed on a musical style, but when it came to dress they were one and the same. The American musician Richard Hell started the craze for facial piercings and safety pins. This painful-looking style still works: in McQueen's new menswear collection, models wore a large safety pin on the face (truly, it looks agonizing).

These looks were also used to make political statements, and punk fashion evolved into the familiar style of today, including the Mohawk David Beckham wore in 2000, studded collars and tattoos.

Later, Jean Paul Gaultier and Zandra Rhodes also designed punk fashion, and punk made it onto the runway. More and more brands now trade on punk: Too Fast, Living Dead Souls, Cyberdog, Demonia, Tripp, Lip Service, Iron Fist, Dead Threads, Morbid Threads, Spin Doctor, Criminal Damage, Hell Bunny, Visual Kei, Hot Topic and Banned are all punk fashion brands (can you tell from their names?).

Yes, punk became fashion, and that meant it lost its original meaning; the value of being your true self faded. "In the '70s and '80s, the punk look marked your identity and declared your beliefs. Above all, it told friend from foe. Later that changed," said Chris Morris, a writer for Billboard and a Hollywood journalist.

## Why the angry young people disappeared

As we said at the start, the "punk" we hear today is the pop-punk of Avril and Sum 41, and the punk-looking people on the street are just following fashion. The anger and rebellion of that era are gone. This punk no longer attacks the problems of its time, nor even expresses what people truly feel. Because it is a business, it has to be popular, and it has to keep repeating what people like most.

The deepest cause, though, is the age structure of the population. Most countries now face an aging population. In 2006, the world had 688 million people aged 60 or over, and the number is still rising. Europe, one of punk's birthplaces, is the most extreme case: in 2004, of the 20 countries with the highest share of people over 60, all but Japan were in Europe.

Low birth rates are another problem there. In many European countries, births now fall far short of deaths. In Spain, Greece, Poland, Germany and Sweden, women have fewer than 1.4 children each on average. At that rate, the populations of many European countries will shrink by a fifth or more by 2040.

In a society this old, where would you find enough angry young people to play punk together and say no together?

As the share of young people falls, the middle class keeps growing, and people have gradually adopted middle-class ways of thinking and living, which are steeped in refinement, caution and stability. Punk, by contrast, wants to smash every existing constraint and rule and to assert whatever it feels, whatever the consequences. In this contest, the middle class has won: commerce wore down the punk spirit, and a comfortable, easy life became people's daily reality, or at least their goal.

Young people are no longer angry, or at least they no longer dare to be so angry. Even when someone wants to fight something, they may not find enough people to back them, and the protest loses steam.

Anger may also have moved elsewhere. The rise of the internet and social networks has given more subcultures their own hidden corners and given anger many new forms; it no longer has to be broadcast through something as public as music. And in some places, censorship helps a great deal: some people stay silent out of confusion and cynicism, others out of fear.

Still, punk has not vanished entirely. It survives in corners of the world. 1990s is a fine punk band: on its 2007 album *Cookies*, it sang its devil-may-care attitude in the most classic punk style.

In 2015, Vogue threw a punk-themed party. The room was full of gowns, and guests politely clinked glasses and chatted. Grace Coddington, then the magazine's creative director, looked around and said: "Look around. Nobody here is a punk."

![1990s: *Cookies*](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702160819LFwYURcxN4oAleJv.jpg-w600)
